description: Independent fact-check of the research claims behind docs/architecture/vlm-annotation-qa-design.md. H.. = high-importance research claims; D.. = claims disputed by the design-review judges. Appendix A of the design document cites the corrected_claim wording.

verdicts.evidence: Full text (ar5iv rendering of arXiv 2008.08115), Section 3.4 'Unavoidable Errors': "Examining the top errors more closely, we find that indeed (at least in COCO), many of the most confident errors are actually misannotated or ambiguously misannotated ground truth (see Fig. 7). For instance, 30 of the top 100 most confident localization errors in Mask R-CNN detections are due to bad annotations, while the number soars to 50 out of 100 for background error." Section 2.2 'Defining Error Types': "The foreground IoU threshold is denoted as t_f and the background threshold is denoted as t_b, which are set to 0.5 and 0.1 (as in [14]) unless otherwise noted." Appendix 0.D adds that for the 'both' error type two thirds of the top 100 were misannotated. Venue confirmed on the ECVA proceedings page (849_ECCV_2020_paper.php) listing title, authors Daniel Bolya, Sean Foley, James Hays, Judy Hoffman, and 'ECCV 2020'; also Springer DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-58580-8_33 (Computer Vision - ECCV 2020). Every figure in the claim (30/100, 50/100, 0.5, 0.1, Mask R-CNN, COCO, Bolya et al., ECCV 2020) matches the source.
verdicts.corrected_claim: TIDE (Bolya, Foley, Hays and Hoffman, ECCV 2020; arXiv 2008.08115) defines its error types with a foreground IoU threshold t_f = 0.5 and a background threshold t_b = 0.1, and reports that 30 of the 100 most confident Mask R-CNN localization errors on COCO and 50 of the 100 most confident background errors are due to misannotated or ambiguously annotated ground truth.

verdicts.evidence: Full text of arXiv 2403.18819 (both arxiv.org/html and ar5iv renderings), section 'Imperfections in COCO-2017 masks': "We found 410 pairs of masks that overlap with intersection-over-union (IoU) greater than 0.8 in the COCO-2017 validation set (≈2.3% of all instances)." Table 1 (instance statistics) prints exact integers with no approximation symbol: COCO-2017 val = 36,781 instances; COCO-ReM val = 40,689 instances (difference 3,908). The 2.3% figure is consistent with 410 pairs = 820 masks / 36,781 = 2.23%. Venue: arXiv comments say only 'Technical report', but the paper appears in the ECCV 2024 proceedings — ECVA paper 06053.pdf under eccv_2024, ECCV 2024 virtual poster 1898, and Springer/ACM DL DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-72784-9_16 ('Computer Vision - ECCV 2024'); authors Singh, Yadav, Jain, Shi, Johnson, Desai. cocorem.xyz lists val as '41k+' masks over 5,000 images, consistent with 40,689. All figures in the claim match.
verdicts.corrected_claim: COCO-ReM (Singh et al., ECCV 2024; arXiv 2403.18819) found 410 pairs of masks overlapping with IoU > 0.8 in the COCO-2017 validation set (≈2.3% of all instances), and its refined validation annotations contain 40,689 instances versus 36,781 in COCO-2017 val (Table 1).

verdicts.evidence: Full text of arXiv 2309.00832 (arxiv.org/html and ar5iv renderings agree verbatim). COCO-bench: "This subset of 2171 images from the famous COCO 2017 dataset ... only considers 5 of the classes: person, chair, cup, car, and traffic light." Mislabeled count: "In total, 251 images in COCO-bench are considered mislabeled and we are confident in the ground truth assessments." Adjudication: "for each image, we compared its 5-class COCO annotation to its independent annotation by Ma et al. (2022) and by sama (2022) in order to determine ground truth. When both of these extra annotations disagreed with the COCO annotation but agreed with one another, we considered the image to be mislabeled ... We manually inspected the remaining images to decide which were mislabeled or not." Error-rate estimate: "Through visual examination of many top/mid/bottom-ranking ObjectLab results, we estimate that in COCO 2017 around: 5% of images have an Overlooked error, 3% have a Badly Located error, and 0.7% have a Swapped error." Venue: ICML 2023 Workshop on Data-centric Machine Learning Research (icml.cc/virtual/2023/26919); authors Tkachenko, Thyagarajan, Mueller. All figures in the claim match. Two caveats for citation: (1) the 251 figure came from two independent re-annotation sources plus manual inspection of the remaining ambiguous images, not re-annotation alone; (2) the 5%/3%/0.7% rates are the authors' informal estimates from visually inspecting ObjectLab rankings, not a formal audit of a random sample.
verdicts.corrected_claim: ObjectLab (Tkachenko, Thyagarajan and Mueller, ICML 2023 DMLR Workshop; arXiv 2309.00832) built COCO-bench from 2,171 COCO-2017 images restricted to five classes (person, chair, cup, car, traffic light), adjudicated 251 of them as mislabeled by comparing COCO labels against two independent re-annotations (Ma et al. 2022; Sama 2022) plus manual inspection of the remaining cases, and — based on visual examination of ObjectLab rankings rather than a formal audit — estimates that around 5% of COCO 2017 images have an Overlooked (missing-box) error, 3% a Badly Located box, and 0.7% a Swapped class label.

verdicts.evidence: Primary source arXiv 2503.02897 (v1 submitted 3 Mar 2025). Author block (arxiv.org/html/2503.02897v1): "Hong Lu, Yali Bian & Rahul C. Shah ... Intel Labs, Santa Clara, CA 95054, USA ... {hong.lu, yali.bian, rahul.c.shah}@intel.com". Backbone: "We use the largest CLIP model (ViT-L/14@336px) provided by OpenAI as our base architecture." Box rendering: "we draw magenta boxes (3 pixels thick) directly on the image"; crop: "a square around the bounding box, with the length of the side set to 1.2 to 1.5 times the bounding box size". Bad-box definition: "randomly modifying GT bounding boxes where the position and size deviates from the ground truth with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8". Abstract: "ClipGrader achieves 91% accuracy on COCO with a 1.8% false positive rate ... achieving 79% accuracy across 1,203 classes" (Table 1: COCO 100%: Acc 91%, recall of good labels 84.7%, false acceptance of bad labels 1.8%; LVIS 100%: 79%). Zero-shot: "the ClipGrader model, trained on the COCO dataset ... across over 1100 entirely unseen object classes - it achieved an accuracy of approximately 11%" (note: this is a COCO-trained model evaluated on LVIS classes absent from COCO). Limitation: "it is not trained to find missing annotations in an image, presenting an area for potential future work." Every figure in the claim matches.
verdicts.corrected_claim: ClipGrader (Lu, Bian & Shah, Intel Labs; arXiv 2503.02897, v1 3 Mar 2025) fine-tunes OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14@336px on square crops 1.2-1.5x the box with the candidate box drawn as a 3-pixel magenta rectangle; defining 'bad' boxes as ground-truth perturbations with IoU 0.5-0.8, it reports 91% accuracy (1.8% false-positive rate) on COCO, 79% accuracy on LVIS across 1,203 classes, only about 11% accuracy when the COCO-trained model is applied zero-shot to over 1,100 LVIS classes unseen in training, and the authors state it is not trained to find missing annotations.

verdicts.evidence: Primary source arXiv 2508.06556, 'From Label Error Detection to Correction: A Modular Framework and Benchmark for Object Detection Datasets' (Penquitt, Klees, Cakaj, Kondermann, Rottmann, Schmarje); v1 6 Aug 2025, v2 30 Jan 2026. Verified against both the arXiv HTML and the extracted text of the v1 and v2 PDFs. Dataset (v2 Sec. IV-A): "we randomly split the annotated training set into training (80%) and validation (20%) subsets ... 1,497 validation images with 896 pedestrian annotations" (KITTI's test set has no public labels, so the 'validation images' are a split of the labelled training set; the paper also calls them '1,497 KITTI training images'). Error counts (v2 Sec. V-A, default configuration = box height >= 25 px, intersection-over-box-area < 0.5 with any don't-care region, soft-label probability >= 0.5): "Using this configuration, we identified a total of 384 label errors in the subset of 1,497 KITTI training images (table IV). Out of these, 228 pedestrians were missing entirely and 156 were annotated with inaccurate bounding boxes." Table IV row '>=25pixels, outside Don't Care, p>=0.5': Overlooked 228, Misfitting 156. Misaligned criterion: "Misfitting boxes are VGT annotations for which there is an intersecting bounding box in the original GT, but with an IoU below 0.5" (intersecting => IoU > 0). Spurious: "we still identified several 85 false positives in the original KITTI dataset based on our validated ground truth." Undetected share: abstract "even the best methods still miss up to 66% of the label errors"; body: "up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected. The gap increases under less restrictive matching conditions (e.g., without minimum box size), where up to 66% of FNs go unnoticed." Cost: Table I "Direct box 2833 1.0 44.11" (average seconds per box; keypoint-to-box 92.67, combined 103.79, validated GT 124.75). IMPORTANT VERSION CAVEAT: the same passage in v1 (Aug 2025) reads "a total of 497 label errors ... 398 pedestrians were missing entirely and 159 were annotated with inaccurate bounding boxes" (and v1's own arithmetic, 398+159=557, does not sum to 497); v2 revised these to 384/228/156 (which do sum). The 85 false positives, 1,497 images, 896/1,567 annotation counts, 66%/44% and 44.11 s figures are identical in both versions. The claim's numbers all match v2, which is what the arxiv.org/html URL resolves to.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Rechecked/REC✓D (Penquitt et al., arXiv 2508.06556v2, 30 Jan 2026) validated the KITTI pedestrian class on a 1,497-image validation split (20% of the labelled KITTI training set, 896 original pedestrian boxes) and, under its default configuration (box height >= 25 px, outside 'don't care' regions, soft-label probability >= 0.5), identified 384 label errors — 228 pedestrians missing entirely and 156 with inaccurate boxes (an original box intersects but IoU < 0.5) — plus 85 spurious original boxes; it reports that the best label-error detection methods still leave up to 44% of missing labels undetected under default matching and up to 66% under relaxed matching (the abstract's headline figure), and that direct bounding-box annotation averaged 44.11 s per box (cite v2 specifically: the Aug 2025 v1 reported 497 errors, 398 missing / 159 inaccurate).

verdicts.evidence: Primary source arXiv 1708.02750, 'Extreme clicking for efficient object annotation' (Papadopoulos, Uijlings, Keller, Ferrari), ICCV 2017 (Semantic Scholar: venue 'IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision', 2017, DOI 10.1109/ICCV.2017.528). Verified in both the ar5iv rendering and the extracted text of the arXiv PDF. Sec. 5.1: "Comparing GT Boxes and GT SegBoxes reveals this agreement to be at 88% mIoU on VOC 2007. Moreover, 93% of all GT Boxes have IoU > 0.7 with their corresponding GT SegBox." (GT SegBoxes = boxes fitted to the PASCAL ground-truth segmentation masks.) Table 1, VOC 2007: 'PASCAL GT Boxes' mIoU 88, IoU>0.7 93, time per instance 34.5 s; 'Extreme clicks' mIoU 88, IoU>0.7 92, time per instance 7.0 s (VOC 2012: 7.2 s). Text: "extreme clicks are 5x cheaper: 7.0s instead of 34.5s." Derivation of 34.5 s (Sec. 2): "They report the following median times [62 = Su et al. 2012, ILSVRC protocol]: 25.5s for drawing one box, 9.0s for verifying its quality ... we use 25.5s+9.0s = 34.5s as the reference time. This is a conservative estimate: when taking into account that some boxes are rejected and need to be re-drawn, the median time increases to 55s. If we use average times instead of medians, the cost raises further to 117s." Note the 34.5 s is a literature-derived reference (Su et al. medians), not a time measured by the authors on VOC.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In 'Extreme clicking for efficient object annotation' (Papadopoulos, Uijlings, Keller & Ferrari, ICCV 2017, arXiv 1708.02750), PASCAL VOC 2007 ground-truth boxes agree with boxes fitted to the ground-truth segmentation masks at 88% mIoU and 93% of GT boxes have IoU > 0.7 with their segmentation-derived box, and extreme clicking took 7.0 s per box on VOC 2007 (7.2 s on VOC 2012) versus a 34.5 s reference derived from Su et al.'s (2012) ILSVRC median times of 25.5 s to draw one box plus 9.0 s to verify it.

verdicts.evidence: Qwen3-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2511.21631, v2 dated 27 Nov 2025), §3.2.4 grounding/counting data, p. 7 of the PDF, verbatim: "Different from Qwen2.5-VL, we adopt a normalized coordinate system scaled to the range [0, 1000] in this version. This design improves robustness to variations in image resolution and aspect ratio across diverse inputs, while also simplifying post-processing and enhancing the usability of predicted coordinates in downstream applications." (verified by extracting the PDF text locally with pypdf, and independently via the arXiv HTML fetch and a web search). The Qwen3-VL report itself does not spell out what Qwen2.5-VL used; the 'absolute pixel coordinates' characterisation comes from the Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2502.13923), §2.2.1 titled "Grounding Data with Absolute Position Coordinates": "Qwen2.5-VL uses coordinate values based on the actual dimensions of the input images during training to represent bounding boxes and points", and §2.1.2: "Unlike traditional approaches that normalize coordinates, our model directly uses the actual dimensions of the input image to represent bounding boxes, points, and other spatial features." Both halves of the claim are therefore supported by primary sources; the only nuance is that the parenthetical about Qwen2.5-VL should be cited to the Qwen2.5-VL report, not the Qwen3-VL report.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The Qwen3-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2511.21631, §3.2.4) states: "Different from Qwen2.5-VL, we adopt a normalized coordinate system scaled to the range [0, 1000] in this version", whereas the Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2502.13923, §2.2.1 "Grounding Data with Absolute Position Coordinates") states that Qwen2.5-VL "uses coordinate values based on the actual dimensions of the input images" for bounding boxes and points.

verdicts.evidence: Verified directly against the text of the Qwen3-VL Technical Report PDF (arXiv 2511.21631v2), extracted locally with pypdf. Table 2 (p. 15), caption "Performance of Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B and top-tier models on visual benchmarks", columns = Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B (thinking, instruct), Gemini 2.5 Pro (thinking, budget-128), GPT-5 (high, minimal), Claude Opus 4.1 (thinking, non-thinking); rows: "RefCOCO-avg 92.1 91.9 74.6* - 66.8 - - -" and "ODinW-13 43.2 48.6 33.7* 34.5 - - - -", so Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct = 91.9 RefCOCO-avg and 48.6 ODinW-13 (thinking variant = 92.1 / 43.2). Table 4 (p. 18), caption "Performance of small-sized Qwen3-VL models and GPT-5-nano on visual benchmarks", columns = Qwen3-VL-2B (thinking, instruct), 4B (thinking, instruct), 8B (thinking, instruct), GPT-5 nano (high, minimal); rows: "RefCOCO-avg 84.8 85.6 88.2 89.0 88.2 89.1 - -" and "ODinW-13 36.0 43.4 39.4 48.2 39.8 44.7 - -", so Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct = 89.1 RefCOCO-avg and 44.7 ODinW-13 mAP (note: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct scores higher on ODinW-13 at 48.2). §5.5 (p. 19), verbatim: "For ODinW-13, we adopt mean Average Precision (mAP) as the evaluation metric by setting confidence scores to 1.0. To ensure comparability with conventional open-set object detection specialist models, we provide all dataset categories simultaneously within the prompt during evaluation. As shown in Table 2, our flagship model, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B ... achieves 48.6 mAP on ODinW-13". Caution for the design doc: an automated summary of the ar5iv rendering returned different figures ("Table 9", 8B = 88.3/38.5, 235B = 92.2/48.6); those are extraction errors, and the PDF text above is authoritative.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In the Qwen3-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2511.21631v2), Table 4 reports Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 89.1 RefCOCO-avg and 44.7 mAP on ODinW-13 (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct: 89.0 / 48.2), and Table 2 reports Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct at 91.9 RefCOCO-avg and 48.6 ODinW-13 mAP, with ODinW-13 mAP computed by setting confidence scores to 1.0 and providing all dataset categories simultaneously in the prompt (§5.5).

verdicts.evidence: License: the Hugging Face model card OpenGVLab/InternVL3_5-8B lists the license as "apache-2.0" and notes "This project uses the pre-trained Qwen3 as a component, which is licensed under the apache-2.0 License" (the InternVL GitHub repo code is separately MIT-licensed). Grounding numbers: InternVL3.5 paper (arXiv 2508.18265, v1 25 Aug 2025 and v2 27 Aug 2025), Table 7, caption "Comparison of visual grounding performance. We evaluate InternVL3.5's visual grounding capability on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg datasets"; InternVL3.5-8B row: RefCOCO val 92.4 / testA 94.7 / testB 88.7, RefCOCO+ val 87.9 / testA 92.4 / testB 82.4, RefCOCOg val 89.6 / test 89.4, Overall 89.7 (identical in v1 and v2; InternVL3-8B for comparison: 92.5 / 88.2 / 89.6, overall 89.6). Nuance: 'overall 89.7' is the mean over all eight splits ((92.4+94.7+88.7+87.9+92.4+82.4+89.6+89.4)/8 = 89.69), not the mean of the three val figures (which would be 90.0). Output format: not described in the InternVL3.5 paper itself; it is documented in the InternVL tutorial "Chat Data Format" page: format "<ref>class name</ref><box>[[x1, y1, x2, y2], ...]</box>" and "We normalize each coordinate box to the range [0, 1000] using the width and height of the image, and round the normalized coordinates to integers" (example: "<ref>the lady with the blue shirt</ref><box>[[243, 469, 558, 746]]</box>"), and the official RefCOCO evaluation script internvl_chat/eval/refcoco/evaluate_grounding.py prompts with "Please provide the bounding box coordinate of the region this sentence describes: <ref>{}</ref>", parses [[x1,y1,x2,y2]] from the output, and rescales via predict_bbox / 1000 then multiplying by image width/height.
verdicts.corrected_claim: InternVL3.5-8B is published under the Apache-2.0 license (Hugging Face model card) and Table 7 of the InternVL3.5 paper (arXiv 2508.18265) reports RefCOCO val 92.4, RefCOCO+ val 87.9, RefCOCOg val 89.6 with an overall score of 89.7 averaged over all eight RefCOCO/+/g splits; InternVL's documented grounding format (InternVL tutorial docs and official RefCOCO evaluation script, not the paper itself) is <ref>…</ref><box>[[x1, y1, x2, y2]]</box> with coordinates normalized to the 0-1000 range and rounded to integers.

verdicts.evidence: Coordinates page (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision-coordinates) states verbatim: "Claude works best with absolute pixel coordinates." and "Claude does not work well when you ask for normalized coordinates, for example: 'Return bounding box coordinates between 0 and 1000.'" Its resize rule: "Edge limit: neither side exceeds the maximum edge length (1568 px on the standard tier, 2576 px on the high-resolution tier)" and "the image's token cost ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ does not exceed the model's visual token budget (1568 tokens on the standard tier, 4784 on the high-resolution tier)." The tier-to-model mapping is NOT on the coordinates page; it is on the Vision page (…/vision, section 'Resolution and token cost'), whose table reads: "High-resolution | Claude 4.7 and later models | 2576 px | 4784" and "Standard | All other models | 1568 px | 1568", plus "Each patch is a 28×28-pixel block… An image, therefore, costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens." All five figures in the claim match; only the sourcing is split across two pages. Note the Vision page also says the token budget, not the edge limit, usually governs (1920×1080 resizes to 1456×819 on standard tier, not 1568×882).
verdicts.corrected_claim: Anthropic's 'Coordinates and bounding boxes' documentation states that Claude works best with absolute pixel coordinates and 'does not work well' when asked for normalized coordinates such as 0-1000; an image costs ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) visual tokens, and per the companion Vision page's resolution-tier table, standard-tier models ('all other models') cap images at a 1568 px long edge and 1568 visual tokens while high-resolution-tier models ('Claude 4.7 and later models') cap at 2576 px and 4784 visual tokens.

verdicts.evidence: (1) box_2d format CONFIRMED: image-understanding page states verbatim "The box_2d should be [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized to 0-1000." (2) Pricing CONFIRMED: pricing page lists Gemini 3.8 Flash input "$0.75 through December 31, 2026. $1.50 starting January 1, 2027." and output "$3.75 through December 31, 2026. $7.50 starting January 1, 2027." (Batch $0.375/$1.875; Flex same as Batch; Priority $1.35/$6.75; caching $0.075/$0.15). Independently corroborated by DataCamp/OpenRouter/apidog search results. (3) 258-token rule PARTIALLY confirmed: the image-understanding and tokens pages do print "258 tokens if both dimensions <= 384 pixels. Larger images are tiled into 768x768 pixel tiles, each costing 258 tokens." without model qualification. HOWEVER Google's media-resolution page (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/media-resolution), whose code samples use gemini-3.8-flash, gives a Gemini 3 image token table: unspecified (Default) 1120, low 280, medium 560, high 1120, ultra_high 2240, and says "The token count for this level varies significantly between Gemini 3 and earlier Gemini models." The pricing page likewise prices Gemini 3.1 Flash Image input at "560 tokens … per image", not 258. So pairing the 258-tokens-per-tile figure with Gemini 3.8 Flash pricing, as the claim does, would understate per-image cost by roughly 4x at default resolution; the 258 rule is legacy text that Google's own 3.x documentation supersedes. The 3.8 Flash model page itself lists no tokens-per-image figure.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Gemini's image-understanding docs define box_2d as [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized to 0-1000; the docs still print a legacy image-token rule (258 tokens if both dimensions are <= 384 px, otherwise 258 tokens per 768x768 tile), but Google's media-resolution page states that Gemini 3-family models instead allocate 280 (low), 560 (medium), 1120 (high, the default) or 2240 (ultra_high) tokens per input image via the media_resolution parameter, so 3.8 Flash cost estimates should use those figures; the Gemini API pricing page lists Gemini 3.8 Flash at $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens through December 31, 2026, rising to $1.50/$7.50 on January 1, 2027 (Batch tier $0.375/$1.875).

verdicts.evidence: Two independent reads of playground.roboflow.com/evals plus the task page /evals/object-detection all return the claimed figures exactly: GPT-6 Astra 82.1%, Qwen3.8 Max 76.7%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 70.6%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 67.4%, Claude Fable 5.1 61.4%, Qwen3.6 27B 59.7%; date text "Evals updated September 5, 2026"; headline metric mAP@50 (task page: "mAP@50 requires 50% overlap, mAP@75 requires 75%, and mAP@50:95 averages across thresholds"). IMPORTANT QUALIFIERS the claim omits: (a) the summary leaderboard reports the LOW reasoning-effort pass: "Every table on this site other than a task leaderboard, including the Average column, uses the low-effort pass so all models are compared on the same amount of compute." The task page's high-effort rows score differently: GPT-6 Astra (high) 83.6%, Qwen3.8 Max (high) 78.4%, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) 74.8%, Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) 74.3%, Claude Fable 5.1 (high) 65.0%, Gemini 3.5 Flash (high) 69.8%. (b) The six listed models are not consecutively ranked: Gemini 3.7 Flash 70.5%, GPT-5.6 Sol 68.4%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 68.1% and Qwen3.8 27B 65.7% (all low) sit between them. (c) 'Qwen3.6 27B' appears twice on the task table (59.7% and 53.9%, both labelled low); the model page gives API/FP8 59.7%, self-hosted BF16 58.0%, AWQ INT4 61.1%. (d) The leaderboard is a moving snapshot: a third-party mirror (BenchmarkList, 403 on direct fetch) indexed a Sep 2, 2026 version with Qwen3.8 Max at 77.1% over 36 models.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Roboflow's Vision Evals object-detection leaderboard ('Evals updated September 5, 2026'; headline metric mAP@50, reported at the low reasoning-effort setting so all models use comparable compute) scores GPT-6 Astra 82.1%, Qwen3.8 Max 76.7%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 70.6%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 67.4%, Claude Fable 5.1 61.4% and Qwen3.6 27B 59.7%, with other models (e.g. Gemini 3.7 Flash 70.5%, GPT-5.6 Sol 68.4%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 68.1%) interleaved between them; at high reasoning effort GPT-6 Astra reaches 83.6% and Claude Fable 5.1 65.0%.

verdicts.evidence: GitHub README (facebookresearch/sam3): "SAM 3 consists of a detector and a tracker that share a vision encoder. It has 848M parameters."; "The detector is a DETR-based model conditioned on text, geometry, and image exemplars."; outputs via `masks, boxes, scores = output["masks"], output["boxes"], output["scores"]`; "This project is licensed under the SAM License"; "please request access to the checkpoints on the SAM 3 Hugging Face repo." README image table: SAM 3 COCO AP 56.4 vs DINO-X 56.0; LVIS AP (Box) 53.6 vs DINO-X 52.4 (LVIS mask AP is 48.5 vs 38.5); SA-Co/Gold cgF1 (mask) 54.1 vs DINO-X 21.3, Human 72.8 (box-column variant: SAM 3 55.7 vs DINO-X 22.5). Meta SAM 3.1 blog: "SAM 3 supports ... concept prompts such as simple noun phrases and image exemplars, as well as visual prompts, such as masks, boxes, and points." Release date: Meta newsroom post about.fb.com/news/2025/11/... dated November 19, 2025 ("we're sharing the SAM 3 model weights"); HF LICENSE file titled "SAM License" with effective date November 19, 2025; arXiv 2511.16719 v1 submitted Nov 20, 2025. verdicts.evidence: arXiv 2503.02897 (Lu, Bian, Shah; Intel Labs; submitted Mar 3, 2025), verbatim from the HTML: "draw magenta boxes (3 pixels thick) directly on the image"; "dynamically crop the image in a square around the bounding box, with the length of the side set to 1.2 to 1.5 times the bounding box size"; "We use the largest CLIP model (ViT-L/14@336px) provided by OpenAI as our base architecture."; bad boxes generated by "randomly modifying GT bounding boxes where the position and size deviates from the ground truth with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8"; Table 1 (COCO, 100% training data): 91% accuracy, 84.7% "Mean recall of good labels", 1.8% "Mean false acceptance (false positives) of bad labels"; abstract: "achieves 91% accuracy on COCO with a 1.8% false positive rate" and "79% accuracy across 1,203 classes" on LVIS; zero-shot: "across over 1100 entirely unseen object classes - it achieved an accuracy of approximately 11%"; also "remove objects that have bounding boxes with both height and width smaller than 20 pixels" and "it is not trained to find missing annotations".
verdicts.corrected_claim: ClipGrader (Lu, Bian & Shah, Intel Labs, arXiv 2503.02897, March 2025) renders each candidate annotation as a 3-pixel-thick magenta box and crops a square 1.2-1.5x the box size, fine-tunes OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14@336px, defines 'bad' boxes as ground-truth perturbations with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8, and reports on COCO 91% accuracy with 84.7% mean recall of good labels and 1.8% mean false acceptance of bad labels, 79% accuracy on LVIS (1,203 classes), and only about 11% accuracy on over 1,100 unseen LVIS classes.

verdicts.evidence: Paper exists: arXiv 2606.13156, Tripathy & Krishnan. All quantitative findings verified verbatim in v2: abstract "the trained model surpasses the single-shot base by +2.4pp Acc@0.5. We show this gain is a measurement mirage ... stopping at step 0 matches the base and beats every shippable rule ... Self-verification confidence correlates only weakly with correctness (r about 0.22)"; body: "Confidence is only weakly correlated with actual step IoU (Pearson r=0.229 for SFT, 0.223 for GRPO)"; Table 1: base 0.796 Acc@0.5 vs SFT+IVT 0.820 (oracle best-step selection); base model Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on a 1:1:1 mix of RefCOCOg, Ref-Adv-S and Ref-L4 (505 test). Attribution issue: the title 'Iterative Visual Thinking and the Self-Correction Mirage in VLM Grounding' and the mirage/r≈0.22/step-0 findings belong to v2, submitted 6 July 2026 (page footer: arXiv:2606.13156v2 [cs.CV] 06 Jul 2026). v1 (11 June 2026) was titled 'Iterative Visual Thinking: Teaching Vision-Language Models Spatial Self-Correction through Visual Feedback', reported "Acc@0.5 rises to 82.0% (+2.4pp)" as a positive result, and did not mention r≈0.22 or 'mirage'. Calling it 'the June 2026 paper' points to the wrong version.
verdicts.corrected_claim: 'Iterative Visual Thinking and the Self-Correction Mirage in VLM Grounding' (Tripathy & Krishnan, arXiv 2606.13156v2, July 2026; v1 June 2026 under a different title) finds, for Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on a RefCOCOg/Ref-Adv-S/Ref-L4 mix, that VLM self-verification confidence correlates only weakly with box correctness (Pearson r≈0.22; 0.229 SFT, 0.223 GRPO) and that the apparent +2.4 pp Acc@0.5 gain from iterative box refinement (0.796 to 0.820) depends on oracle best-step selection and vanishes under label-free stopping rules: 'stopping at step 0 matches the base and beats every shippable rule'.

verdicts.evidence: The cited Open Images V7 facts page (factsfigures_v7.html) confirms every element except the scoping of the 90% figure. Verbatim: "90% of the boxes were manually drawn by professional annotators at Google using the efficient extreme clicking interface"; "We produced the remaining 10% semi-automatically using an enhanced version of the method"; "These boxes have been human verified to have IoU>0.7 with a perfect box on the object, and in practice they are accurate (mean IoU ~0.77". However, a second targeted read shows these sentences sit in the TRAINING-set paragraph (Table 2: training 14,610,229 boxes on 1,743,042 images; validation 303,980 boxes; test 937,327 boxes), while for validation/test the page states "All boxes were manually drawn." The overall total is 15,851,536 boxes (index.html: "15,851,536 boxes on 600 classes"), so "16M" is a fair rounding, but "90% of its 16M boxes" mis-scopes a statement made about the 14.6M training boxes (the overall manual share is ~91% once the fully-manual val/test splits are included). License text confirmed verbatim on the same page in two independent reads: "The annotations are licensed by Google LLC under CC BY 4.0 license. The images are listed as having a CC BY 2.0 license. Note: while we tried to identify images that are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution license, we make no representations or warranties regarding the license status of each image and you should verify the license for each image yourself." The Open Images V4 paper abstract (arXiv 1811.00982) corroborates scale ("15.4M bounding boxes for 600 object classes" at V4) but does not itself state the 90% figure.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Open Images V7 annotations are licensed by Google LLC under CC BY 4.0; its images are "listed as having a CC BY 2.0 license" with an explicit disclaimer that Google makes no representations or warranties about each image's license status; of its 15.85M bounding boxes (600 classes), the 14.6M training-set boxes were 90% manually drawn by professional annotators at Google using extreme clicking, with the remaining 10% produced semi-automatically and human-verified to have IoU>0.7 with a perfect box (mean IoU ~0.77), while all validation and test boxes were manually drawn.

verdicts.evidence: Both arxiv.org/html/2309.00832 and ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2309.00832 (ObjectLab: Automated Diagnosis of Mislabeled Images in Object Detection Data; Tkachenko, Thyagarajan, Mueller; arXiv v1 submitted 2 Sep 2023 — a v2 URL returns HTTP 404, so v1 is the only version) contain the exact figures. Verbatim: "Through visual examination of many top/mid/bottom-ranking ObjectLab results, we estimate that in COCO 2017 around: 5% of images have an Overlooked error, 3% have a Badly Located error, and 0.7% have a Swapped error." On the benchmark: "This subset of 2171 images from the famous COCO 2017 dataset ... only considers 5 of the classes: person, chair, cup, car, and traffic light." and "In total, 251 images in COCO-bench are considered mislabeled and we are confident in the ground truth assessments." Adjudication: "When both of these extra annotations disagreed with the COCO annotation but agreed with one another, we considered the image to be mislabeled ... When all three annotations agreed, we considered the image correctly labeled. Here agreement between annotations was assessed by thresholding their pairwise mAP score. We manually inspected the remaining images to decide which were mislabeled or not." Caveat: the 5%/3%/0.7% numbers are an informal estimate from visual inspection of ObjectLab's ranked outputs, not a full independent audit of COCO; the paper's term for incorrect class labels is "Swapped" error. The arXiv abstract page itself does not carry these numbers (they are in the body).
verdicts.corrected_claim: ObjectLab (Tkachenko, Thyagarajan & Mueller, arXiv 2309.00832, Sep 2023) estimates from visual examination of its ranked results that roughly 5% of COCO 2017 images contain an Overlooked (missing-box) error, 3% a Badly Located box, and 0.7% a Swapped (incorrect class) label; its COCO-bench benchmark comprises 2,171 COCO 2017 images restricted to 5 classes (person, chair, cup, car, traffic light), of which 251 images were adjudicated as mislabeled using two additional independent annotations plus manual inspection.

verdicts.evidence: Full text of Papadopoulos et al., 'Extreme clicking for efficient object annotation' (ICCV 2017, arXiv 1708.02750), Section 5.1 'Results on quality and efficiency' (via ar5iv): 'Having two sets of ground-truth boxes enables us to measure the agreement among the expert annotators that created PASCAL. Comparing GT Boxes and GT SegBoxes reveals this agreement to be at 88% mIoU on VOC 2007.' and 'Moreover, 93% of all GT Boxes have IoU >0.7 with their corresponding GT SegBox.' and 'In terms of annotation efficiency, extreme clicks are 5x cheaper: 7.0s instead of 34.5s.' The 'two sets' are the official VOC 2007 GT boxes and 'GT SegBoxes', defined as 'bounding boxes which we fit to the ground-truth segmentations'. The 34.5 s figure is the Su et al. ILSVRC protocol cost of '25.5s for drawing one box, 9.0s for verifying its quality' (the additional 7.8 s coverage check is excluded), so 'draw-plus-verify' is the correct description. The arXiv abstract independently states 'annotation time is only 7s per box, 5x faster than the traditional way of drawing boxes'. All four figures (88%, 93%/0.7, 7.0 s, 34.5 s) match the claim exactly.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In 'Extreme clicking for efficient object annotation' (Papadopoulos et al., ICCV 2017, arXiv 1708.02750, Sec. 5.1), the official PASCAL VOC 2007 ground-truth boxes agree with boxes fitted to the VOC ground-truth segmentations at 88% mean IoU, 93% of GT boxes have IoU > 0.7 with their segmentation-derived box, and extreme clicking costs 7.0 s per box versus 34.5 s (25.5 s drawing + 9.0 s quality verification) for the conventional draw-then-verify protocol.

verdicts.evidence: Paper exists: 'From Label Error Detection to Correction: A Modular Framework and Benchmark for Object Detection Datasets' (Penquitt, Klees et al., arXiv 2508.06556; v1 Aug 6 2025, v2 Jan 30 2026), which introduces 'REC✓D (Rechecked)'. Counts confirmed verbatim from the v2 HTML: 'The resulting dataset consists of 5,984 training images with 3,591 pedestrian objects and 1,497 validation images with 896 pedestrian annotations' (an 80/20 random split the authors made of the KITTI training set, not an official KITTI split); 'The resulting VGT contains 1,567 annotations for the class pedestrian, which is 671 more than in the original GT'; 'Out of these, 228 pedestrians were missing entirely and 156 were annotated with inaccurate bounding boxes'; 'we still identified several 85 false positives in the original KITTI dataset' (Supplementary C-2); 'we identified a total of 384 label errors in the subset of 1,497 KITTI training images'. Detector gap confirmed: 'up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected' in the main setting and 'where up to 66% of FNs go unnoticed' under less restrictive matching; the abstract phrases this as 'up to 66% of the label errors'. GitHub URL confirmed: 'Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/JonathanKlees/rechecked' and the repo README says it contains the validated pedestrian annotations. NOT confirmed: the 'CC BY 4.0' license. The only CC BY 4.0 on the arXiv page is the paper's own arXiv license header ('License: CC BY 4.0'); the paper contains no license statement for the released annotations, and the repository's LICENSE file reads 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2025 Jonathan Klees' with no CC BY mention. Note also that KITTI itself is 'published under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 License' (cvlibs.net), which constrains any derived annotations.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The REC✓D/Rechecked benchmark (arXiv 2508.06556, v2 Jan 2026) validated the KITTI pedestrian class on a 1,497-image validation split with 896 original annotations, producing 1,567 validated boxes and identifying 228 missing pedestrians, 156 inaccurate boxes and 85 spurious labels (384 label errors), and reports that the best existing detectors still leave up to 44% (main setting) to 66% (relaxed matching) of missing labels undetected; the code and validated annotations are at github.com/JonathanKlees/rechecked under an MIT code license (the paper states no separate data license, and CC BY 4.0 is only the arXiv paper license; KITTI's own terms are CC BY-NC-SA 3.0).

verdicts.evidence: arXiv 2508.06556 (Penquitt, Klees, Cakaj, Kondermann, Rottmann, Schmarje; v1 6 Aug 2025, v2 30 Jan 2026). Abstract: "We detect 18% of missing and inaccurate labels in the original ground truth ... even the best methods still miss up to 66% of the label errors." Body: "the base models saturate at 186 (YOLOX) and 260 (Cascade R-CNN) FNs, while the VGT contains 330 FNs. This indicates that up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected. The gap increases under less restrictive matching conditions (e.g., without minimum box size), where up to 66% of FNs go unnoticed." So the 44%/66% figures specifically concern missing boxes (false negatives); 44% is under the default/stricter matching (IoU 0.5, min 25 px height). Table I ("Bounding box annotation strategies ... Costs are reported as average per box in seconds"): Direct box 44.11 s, Keypoint-to-box 92.67 s, Combined box 103.79 s. Table II (semantic validation, per box): Is pedestrian? 37.87 s, Is human & stand/walk? 57.03 s, with ambiguity refinement 77.85 s, full validated-GT pipeline 124.75 s. All numbers in the claim are present; the 44.11-103.79 range covers the box-drawing microtasks only, and the exact denominator behind the 18% figure is not stated in the abstract.
verdicts.corrected_claim: The Rechecked benchmark (arXiv 2508.06556, v2 revised 30 January 2026) reports that at least 18% of the original KITTI pedestrian labels were missing or inaccurate, that even the best label-error detection methods leave up to 44% of missing boxes undetected under the default matching (IoU 0.5, min 25 px height) and up to 66% under less restrictive matching, and that its bounding-box drawing microtasks cost 44.11 s (direct box), 92.67 s (keypoint-to-box) and 103.79 s (combined) per box, with semantic-validation microtasks at 37.87-77.85 s and the full validated-GT pipeline at 124.75 s per box.

verdicts.evidence: arXiv 2503.02897 (Lu, Bian, Shah; submitted 3 March 2025). Full text: "We use the largest CLIP model (ViT-L/14@336px) provided by OpenAI as our base architecture"; "we draw magenta boxes (3 pixels thick) directly on the image"; "we dynamically crop the image in a square around the bounding box, with the length of the side set to 1.2 to 1.5 times the bounding box size"; bad boxes "are generated by randomly modifying GT bounding boxes where the position and size deviates from the ground truth with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8." Abstract: "ClipGrader achieves 91% accuracy on COCO with a 1.8% false positive rate ... achieving 79% accuracy across 1,203 classes" on LVIS. Table 1 row "COCO 100% | 91% | 84.7% | 1.8%" where the third metric is defined as "Mean false acceptance (false positives) of bad labels", so 'false positive' = accepting a bad label. Every figure in the claim matches.
verdicts.corrected_claim: ClipGrader (Lu, Bian & Shah, arXiv 2503.02897, submitted 3 March 2025) fine-tunes OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14@336px on images where the candidate box is drawn as a 3-pixel magenta rectangle and the image is cropped to a square 1.2-1.5x the box size; 'bad' boxes are ground-truth perturbations with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8, and the model reaches 91% accuracy on COCO with 84.7% recall of good labels and 1.8% false acceptance of bad labels, and 79% accuracy on LVIS across 1,203 classes.

verdicts.evidence: Primary source (arXiv 2003.01285 PDF, text extracted locally; Li, Xiong, Socher, Hoi 2020). Table 2 header rows verbatim: 'BBox Noise 0% 20% 40%' / 'Label Noise 0% 20% 40% 60% 0% 20% 40% 60% 0% 20% 40% 60%' / 'Vanilla [35,6] 78.2 72.9 69.3 62.1 75.5 70.7 66.9 61.2 59.3 54.2 50.0 45.9'. Table 1 (bbox noise 20%/40% only, label 0/20/40): 'vanilla [35,6] 75.5 70.7 66.9 59.3 54.2 50.0'. So: clean (0% bbox, 0% label) = 78.2, NOT 75.5; 75.5 is 20% bbox noise with 0% label noise; 59.3 is 40% bbox noise (0% label), NOT 20% bbox noise; 50.0 is 40% bbox + 40% label noise, NOT 20% bbox + 40% label (that cell is 66.9). All three numbers in the claim are misattributed. The parts that do check out: noise model — 'we perturb the coordinates of all bounding boxes by a number of pixels uniformly drawn from [−wNb%, +wNb%] (w is bbox width) for horizontal coordinates or [−hNb%, +hNb%] (h is bbox height) for vertical coordinates'; label noise — 'randomly choose Nl% of the training samples and change each of their labels to another random label'; backbone — 'Faster-RCNN [35] architecture with ResNet-50 [18] and FPN [25] as the feature extractor', implemented in mmdetection; training on VOC 2007+2012 trainval, evaluated mAP@.5 on VOC 2007 test. Also useful: 'Under 40% bbox noise, the average IoU between a noisy bbox and its corresponding clean bbox is only 0.45.' Note: two WebFetch summaries of ar5iv returned contradictory column mappings; the locally extracted PDF text is authoritative.
verdicts.corrected_claim: In Li et al. (arXiv 2003.01285, 2020, Table 2), a vanilla Faster R-CNN (ResNet-50 + FPN, mmdetection) trained on VOC07+12 trainval and evaluated on VOC 2007 test scores 78.2 mAP@0.5 with clean annotations; with box noise alone (each coordinate shifted by a pixel offset drawn uniformly from ±N_b% of box width/height) it drops to 75.5 at N_b=20% and 59.3 at N_b=40%, and with 40% symmetric label noise added it drops to 66.9 (20% box noise) and 50.0 (40% box noise); at 40% box noise the mean IoU between noisy and clean boxes is only 0.45.

verdicts.evidence: Qwen3-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2511.21631, submitted 26 Nov 2025, Bai et al.), Section 3.2.4 'Grounding and Counting', verbatim: 'Different from Qwen2.5-VL, we adopt a normalized coordinate system scaled to the range [0,1000] in this version.' (The claim's quote is accurate but truncates the trailing 'in this version'.) The report says this improves robustness across image resolutions/aspect ratios and simplifies post-processing. The Qwen3-VL GitHub README corroborates ('Using relative position coordinates, it supports both boxes and points'). Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2502.13923), Section 2.1.2: 'our model directly uses the actual dimensions of the input image to represent bounding boxes, points, and other spatial features'; Section 2.2.1 'Grounding Data with Absolute Position Coordinates': 'relative coordinates fail to effectively represent the original size and position of objects within images' and it uses 'coordinate values based on the actual dimensions of the input images during training to represent bounding boxes and points', contrasting with the normalized coordinates used by Qwen2-VL. The 'input image' in Qwen2.5-VL is the image after the processor's resize to multiples of 28, so the claim's '(resized)' parenthetical is consistent with the paper, though the paper itself says 'actual dimensions of the input image'.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Qwen3-VL outputs grounding boxes and points in a normalized coordinate system scaled to [0, 1000] — the Qwen3-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2511.21631, §3.2.4) states 'Different from Qwen2.5-VL, we adopt a normalized coordinate system scaled to the range [0,1000] in this version' — whereas Qwen2.5-VL (arXiv 2502.13923, §2.1.2/§2.2.1) 'directly uses the actual dimensions of the input image to represent bounding boxes, points, and other spatial features', i.e. absolute pixel coordinates in the (resized) input-image space rather than the normalized coordinates of Qwen2-VL.

verdicts.evidence: Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report (arXiv 2502.13923), Section 2.1: "During both training and inference, the height and width of the input images are resized to multiples of 28 before being fed into the ViT." Same section: "The vision encoder processes images by splitting them into patches with a stride of 14" and the MLP merger "first group[s] spatially adjacent sets of four patch features... concatenated and passed through a two-layer multi-layer perceptron" (i.e., 2x2 merge). Section 2.2.1 (Grounding Data): "relative coordinates fail to effectively represent the original size and position of objects within images. To address this limitation, Qwen2.5-VL uses coordinate values based on the actual dimensions of the input images during training to represent bounding boxes and points." The rescale-to-original step is confirmed by the official Qwen2.5-VL cookbook spatial_understanding.ipynb at pre-rename commit f61c3cd (2025-01-29): input_height = inputs['image_grid_thw'][0][1]*14; input_width = inputs['image_grid_thw'][0][2]*14; abs_x1 = int(bounding_box["bbox_2d"][0]/input_width * width); abs_y1 = int(bounding_box["bbox_2d"][1]/input_height * height), with min_pixels default 512*28*28 and max_pixels 2048*28*28. The HF model card also states dimensions "will be rounded to the nearest multiple of 28." Note: the paper says 'four adjacent patch features', not literally '2x2'; and the paper itself does not spell out the rescaling — that comes from the official cookbook.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Qwen2.5-VL resizes input image height and width to multiples of 28 before the ViT (patch stride 14, with four spatially adjacent patch features merged by an MLP), and represents boxes with absolute coordinates "based on the actual dimensions of the input images"; the official Qwen2.5-VL cookbook therefore derives the model-seen size as image_grid_thw[.,1]*14 x image_grid_thw[.,2]*14 and rescales predicted boxes by (coord / input_size) * original_size to map them back to the original image.

verdicts.evidence: Perception-R1 (arXiv 2504.07954, single version v1, 10 Apr 2025). Table 5 (Ablation Study) rows: 'w thinking' RefCOCO 75.1 / RefCOCO+ 67.9 / RefCOCOg 71.3; 'w/o thinking' 89.1 / 81.7 / 85.7 — all six numbers match. Text: "Comparative analysis of row 3 and 4 reveals consistent performance degradation across all four evaluated perception tasks when incorporating an explicit thinking process during both training and inference phases." Table 7: "visual grounding | RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg | 320k | 5k | 1.56%" — 5k samples confirmed. verdicts.evidence: Primary docs confirm every element. labelstud.io/guide/predictions: "For image pre-annotations, Label Studio expects the x, y, width, and height of image annotations to be provided in percentages of overall image dimension." Its rectanglelabels example JSON has "predictions": [{"model_version": "one", "score": 0.5, "result": [{"type": "rectanglelabels", ... "original_width": 600, "original_height": 403, "image_rotation": 0, "value": {"rotation": 0, "x": 4.98, "y": 12.82, "width": 32.52, "height": 44.91, "rectanglelabels": ["Airplane"]}}]}]. labelstud.io/tags/rectanglelabels describes value.x as "x coordinate of the top left corner before rotation (0-100)" (same for y/width/height). labelstud.io/guide/export gives the conversion "pixel_x = x / 100.0 * original_width". labelstud.io/guide/task_format: "predictions.score: The overall score of the result, based on the probabilistic output, confidence level, or other." Region-level score: the predictions page's NER example carries "score": 0.70 inside each result's value, and the Label Studio frontend Result model (web/libs/editor/src/regions/Result.js, develop) declares `score: types.maybeNull(types.number)` on every result and serializes it (`if (typeof score === "number") data.score = score;`); the labeling guide offers "Order by Score" for regions. verdicts.corrected_claim: Label Studio stores rectangle regions with value.x, value.y, value.width and value.height expressed as percentages (0-100) of the image dimensions, with original_width and original_height (pixels) stored on each result; predictions carry a model_version string and an overall score, and each result/region may optionally carry its own numeric score field (labelstud.io/guide/predictions; labelstud.io/tags/rectanglelabels; Result.js in the Label Studio frontend).

verdicts.evidence: Timeout and no-retry are confirmed. labelstud.io/guide/webhooks: "Webhook connections time out after 1 second. You can adjust the timeout by setting an environment variable, WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT." and "Label Studio does not retry webhook connections that fail." Source code at every release tag from 1.13.0 through 1.23.0 (latest release, published 2026-03-13 per the GitHub releases API) has `WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT = float(get_env('WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT', 1.0))` in label_studio/core/settings/base.py; webhooks/utils.py passes `timeout=settings.WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT` to a single ssrf_safe_post with no retry loop. NOTE: the unreleased develop branch (as of 2026-09-13) changes the default to `float(get_env('WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT', 10.0))` and adds `WEBHOOK_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES = 50`, which auto-disables a webhook after 50 consecutive failures (still no retry). The event list is only partly right. The guide's table lists the 8 human-readable events (Task Created, Task Deleted, Annotation Created, Annotation Updated, Annotation Deleted, Project Created, Project Updated, Project Deleted), but the actual action strings differ from the claim: the WebhookAction enum in label_studio/webhooks/models.py defines PROJECT_CREATED, PROJECT_UPDATED, PROJECT_DELETED, TASKS_CREATED, TASKS_DELETED, ANNOTATION_CREATED, ANNOTATIONS_CREATED, ANNOTATION_UPDATED, ANNOTATIONS_DELETED, LABEL_LINK_CREATED, LABEL_LINK_UPDATED, LABEL_LINK_DELETED — there is no TASK_CREATED, TASK_DELETED or ANNOTATION_DELETED constant, and a grep of the webhooks app (utils.py, api.py, serializers.py, serializers_for_hooks.py, models.py) finds zero occurrences of those singular strings. The API reference 'Get all webhook actions' lists the same plural names plus ANNOTATIONS_CREATED and LABEL_LINK_* (and REVIEW_* for Enterprise). The docs' webhook_reference page does say e.g. "TASKS_CREATED, or if just one task was imported, TASK_CREATED", but that is not reflected in the code. Project-level events additionally require organization-level webhooks to be enabled (ALLOW_ORGANIZATION_WEBHOOKS).
verdicts.corrected_claim: Label Studio webhooks (through the latest release, 1.23.0) time out after 1 second by default (env var WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT; the unreleased develop branch raises this to 10 s and auto-disables a webhook after 50 consecutive failures) and are never retried on failure; the emitted action strings are TASKS_CREATED, TASKS_DELETED, ANNOTATION_CREATED, ANNOTATIONS_CREATED, ANNOTATION_UPDATED, ANNOTATIONS_DELETED, PROJECT_CREATED, PROJECT_UPDATED, PROJECT_DELETED and LABEL_LINK_CREATED/UPDATED/DELETED, with the PROJECT_* events requiring organization-level webhooks to be enabled.

verdicts.evidence: arXiv 2503.02897 (submitted 3 Mar 2025; authors Hong Lu, Yali Bian, Rahul C. Shah, Intel Labs) exists. Abstract (arxiv.org/abs/2503.02897): 'achieves 91% accuracy on COCO with a 1.8% false positive rate' and 'achieving 79% accuracy across 1,203 classes' on LVIS. Full text (arxiv.org/html/2503.02897v1 and ar5iv, two independent fetches): 'Bad bounding boxes: These are generated by randomly modifying GT bounding boxes where the position and size deviates from the ground truth with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8'; 'we remove objects that have bounding boxes with both height and width smaller than 20 pixels'; 'it is not trained to find missing annotations in an image, presenting an area for potential future work'. Backbone: 'We use the largest CLIP model (ViT-L/14@336px)'. Only nuance: the size filter removes objects whose height AND width are both under 20 px, not any object with one dimension under 20 px.
verdicts.corrected_claim: ClipGrader (Lu, Bian & Shah, Intel Labs; arXiv 2503.02897, March 2025) fine-tunes CLIP ViT-L/14@336px to grade bounding-box annotations and reports 91% accuracy with a 1.8% false-positive rate on COCO and 79% accuracy on LVIS (1,203 classes); its 'bad' boxes are random perturbations of ground-truth boxes with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8, objects whose height and width are both smaller than 20 pixels are removed from training/evaluation, and the paper states the model 'is not trained to find missing annotations in an image'.

verdicts.evidence: Paper exists: Schubert et al., 'Identifying Label Errors in Object Detection Datasets by Loss Inspection', WACV 2024, pp. 4582-4591 (mlanthology.org; CVF open-access page returned 403 but is listed in search); arXiv 2303.06999 v3 (19 Dec 2023). Per-error-type AUROC for BDD, Swin-T backbone, original training labels, loss method: Drop 94.92, Flip 99.68, Shift 65.49, Spawn 98.48 — ar5iv fetch explicitly maps these values to 'Swin-T backbone with original training labels' (ResNeSt101/original: 94.52/99.80/65.84/95.80). The claimed 11.5% (VOC) to 47.5% (KITTI) range is correct for the all-error-type evaluation but omits the drops-only evaluations (COCO 61.0%, VOC 71.5%) that the abstract headlines as 'precision ... of up to 71.5%' on public datasets and 97% on the proprietary dataset. verdicts.corrected_claim: In loss-inspection label-error detection (Schubert et al., WACV 2024; arXiv 2303.06999), AUROC on BDD100k with a Swin-T backbone trained on original labels is 65.49 for shifted boxes (perturbed so that IoU with the original label lies in [0.4, 0.7]) versus 94.92 for drops, 99.68 for flips and 98.48 for spawns; when flagging real label errors in public test sets, precision across all error types ranges from 11.5% (VOC) and 15.5% (BDD) to 24.5% (COCO) and 47.5% (KITTI), rising to 61.0% (COCO) and 71.5% (VOC) when only missing-label (drop) errors are counted, and 97% on a proprietary dataset.

verdicts.evidence: Primary source: arXiv 2508.06556 'From Label Error Detection to Correction: A Modular Framework and Benchmark for Object Detection Datasets' (Penquitt, Klees, Cakaj, Kondermann, Rottmann, Schmarje; v1 6 Aug 2025, v2 30 Jan 2026). All figures except one check out verbatim in the v2 HTML and agree with the ar5iv render. Sec. IV-A: 'The resulting dataset consists of 5,984 training images with 3,591 pedestrian objects and 1,497 validation images with 896 pedestrian annotations.' Sec. V-A: 'we identified a total of 384 label errors in the subset of 1,497 KITTI training images... 228 pedestrians were missing entirely and 156 were annotated with inaccurate bounding boxes' and 'The resulting VGT contains 1,567 annotations for the class pedestrian, which is 671 more than in the original GT.' Appendix C1: '85 false positives in the original KITTI dataset based on our validated ground truth.' Default configuration: soft-label probability >= 0.5, box height >= 25 px, intersection-over-box-area < 0.5 with 'don't care' regions. Table II (caption: 'Costs are reported as average per bounding box in seconds'): 'Validated GT' row with ambiguity refinement = 124.75 s; Table I: direct box 44.11 s, combined box 103.79 s. Sec. V-B verbatim: 'Most detection-based approaches including YOLOX, Cascade R-CNN, and their error detection variants are able to find 150-200 FNs at a cost similar to or lower than the cheapest human annotation strategy. However, the base models saturate at 186 (YOLOX) and 260 (Cascade R-CNN) FNs, while the VGT contains 330 FNs. This indicates that up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected. The gap increases under less restrictive matching conditions (e.g., without minimum box size), where up to 66% of FNs go unnoticed.' DEFECT: the claim attributes '186 of 330 (56%)' to 'the best detection method'. 186 is the YOLOX base model's saturation; Cascade R-CNN saturates at 260 of 330 (79%). The '44% undetected' figure is exactly 1 - 186/330 (YOLOX), i.e. the worse of the two base models, not the best. Minor version notes: the ar5iv (v1) text says the validated GT contains 333 FNs (v2 says 330), and the v1 abstract says 'at least 24% of missing and inaccurate annotations' whereas the v2 abstract says '18%'; cite v2. The GitHub README (JonathanKlees/rechecked, MIT code license) and project page (osvia.org/ReChecked) contain no additional figures.
verdicts.corrected_claim: Rechecked (arXiv 2508.06556v2, Jan 2026) crowd-validated KITTI pedestrian labels on 1,497 validation images, expanding 896 original boxes to 1,567 and finding, under its default configuration (soft-label probability >= 0.5, box height >= 25 px), 384 original errors (228 missing pedestrians, 156 inaccurately localized boxes) plus 85 spurious boxes; detection-based methods recover 150-200 missing boxes at a cost at or below the cheapest human annotation strategy, but the base detectors saturate at 186 (YOLOX) and 260 (Cascade R-CNN) of the 330 missing boxes in the validated ground truth, so up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected (up to 66% under less restrictive matching without a minimum box size); full crowd semantic validation with ambiguity refinement averaged 124.75 s per box versus 44.11 s for direct box annotation.

verdicts.evidence: The paper exists: arXiv 2608.19553v1 (only version; submitted Thu 20 Aug 2026, 1,213 KB), 'Where Grounding Accuracy Lives on the IoU Curve: Label-Free Inference-Time Boundary Refinement', Bo Ma, Auckland University of Technology, marked 'Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027'. Setup (PDF text, Sec. on implementation): 'The generalist arms use a local copy of Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at a single pinned revision', bfloat16, SDPA attention, 'deterministic, non-sampling greedy decoding, at most 64 generated tokens', prompt 'Locate the region that matches: <expression>. Reply only with its bounding box as [x1,y1,x2,y2] in coordinates normalized to 0-1000. No explanation.'; 'We use the complete Ref-L4 test split: 31,921 expressions over 9,467 unique images' (HF dataset card lists the Ref-L4 test split as ~31,900 expressions, consistent). The canonical baseline Acc@0.75 is 77.416%; a superseded routing-only diagnostic in Appendix D.6 quotes 77.410%. An earlier WebFetch summary that reported 77.620 was an extraction error. verdicts.evidence: Primary source arXiv 2503.02897 (submitted 3 Mar 2025; authors Hong Lu, Yali Bian, Rahul C. Shah; affiliation line reads 'Intel Labs, Santa Clara, CA 95054, USA'). Every sub-claim was located verbatim in the arXiv abstract / HTML full text (cross-checked on ar5iv mirror): (1) Abstract: 'ClipGrader achieves 91% accuracy on COCO with a 1.8% false positive rate.' (2) Abstract: 'it maintains 87% accuracy with a 2.1% false positive rate when trained on just 10% of the COCO data'; Sec. 4.1 and Table 1 repeat the 87% figure. (3) Abstract: 'scales effectively to larger datasets such as LVIS, achieving 79% accuracy across 1,203 classes'; Table 1 row 'LVIS 100%' = 79%. (4) Sec. 4.2: 'the ClipGrader model, trained on the COCO dataset, demonstrates a constrained yet significant ability to assess bounding box quality across over 1100 entirely unseen object classes - it achieved an accuracy of approximately 11%.' (Note: this is the COCO-trained model evaluated on LVIS classes absent from COCO, i.e. a zero-shot transfer figure, not a general 'unseen class' rate for the LVIS-trained model.) (5) Sec. 5: 'it is not trained to find missing annotations in an image, presenting an area for potential future work.' (6) Sec. 3.2: 'we draw magenta boxes (3 pixels thick) directly on the image' and 'we dynamically crop the image in a square around the bounding box, with the length of the side set to 1.2 to 1.5 times the bounding box size.' (7) Sec. 3.2: 'Bad bounding boxes: These are generated by randomly modifying GT bounding boxes where the position and size deviates from the ground truth with IoU between 0.5 and 0.8, hence the object class label is correct but the bounding box is not snug.' and 'Background bounding boxes: These are randomly generated bounding boxes that do not have major overlap (i.e. IoU <= 20%) with any labelled objects in the same image.' Good boxes = unmodified GT annotations. Minor caveats for the design doc: the accuracy figures are measured on synthetically perturbed boxes (the paper's own words: 'artificially disturbed bounding boxes'), and there is no separate 'wrong class label' perturbation category in the three-class scheme (good / bad-geometry / background).
verdicts.corrected_claim: ClipGrader (Lu, Bian & Shah, Intel Labs; arXiv 2503.02897, March 2025) fine-tunes CLIP to grade boxes drawn as 3-pixel-thick magenta rectangles on a square crop 1.2-1.5x the box size, using three synthetic classes (good = GT box; bad = perturbed GT box with IoU 0.5-0.8 and correct class; background = random box with IoU <= 0.2 to any labelled object); it reports 91% accuracy at a 1.8% false-positive rate on COCO, 87% / 2.1% when trained on 10% of COCO, 79% accuracy on LVIS (1,203 classes), only ~11% accuracy when the COCO-trained model is applied to >1,100 LVIS classes unseen in training, and it is explicitly not trained to detect missing annotations.

verdicts.evidence: Primary source arXiv 2508.06556 (Penquitt, Klees, Cakaj, Kondermann, Rottmann, Schmarje, 'From Label Error Detection to Correction: A Modular Framework and Benchmark for Object Detection Datasets', submitted 6 Aug 2025, v2 30 Jan 2026; framework/benchmark named REC✓D / 'Rechecked'). CONFIRMED sub-claims (verbatim from arxiv.org/html/2508.06556v2 and ar5iv): (a) '1,497 validation images with 896 pedestrian annotations' — a random 80/20 split of KITTI's annotated training set, so the 1,497 images are the paper's validation split of KITTI's train set (the paper also once calls them 'the subset of 1,497 KITTI training images'); (b) 'The resulting VGT contains 1,567 annotations for the class pedestrian, which is 671 more than in the original GT'; (c) 'we identified a total of 384 label errors ... Out of these, 228 pedestrians were missing entirely and 156 were annotated with inaccurate bounding boxes' — inaccurate is defined as an intersecting original box with IoU below 0.5, missing as IoU of zero, so '0<IoU<0.5' for misaligned is consistent; 384 is the count under the paper's default configuration, so 'at least 384' is a fair reading; (d) 'we still identified ... 85 false positives in the original KITTI dataset based on our validated ground truth'. PARTIALLY WRONG sub-claim: the '66%' statement. Abstract: 'even the best methods still miss up to 66% of the label errors'. Body: 'the base models saturate at 186 (YOLOX) and 260 (Cascade R-CNN) FNs, while the VGT contains 330 FNs. This indicates that up to 44% of missing labels remain undetected. The gap increases under less restrictive matching conditions (e.g., without minimum box size), where up to 66% of FNs go unnoticed.' So 66% applies specifically to missing labels (false negatives) under relaxed matching (no minimum box size); under the default matching the worst case is 44% missed (YOLOX finds 186/330 = 56%, Cascade R-CNN 260/330 = 79%). The claim's paraphrase '<= 34-56% recall' is not supported: recall ranges from ~34% (worst case, lax matching) up to ~79% (Cascade R-CNN, default matching), and the figure is about missing objects, not all error types. Note also the VGT-based FN count under matching (330) differs from the 228 missing found by REC✓D's default configuration. The paper also headline-reports 'We detect 18% of missing and inaccurate labels in the original ground truth', which the claim omits.
verdicts.corrected_claim: REC✓D / Rechecked (Penquitt et al., arXiv 2508.06556, Aug 2025, rev. Jan 2026) re-validated pedestrian labels on a 1,497-image validation split of KITTI's training set: the validated ground truth holds 1,567 pedestrian boxes versus 896 original (671 more), with 384 label errors identified under the default configuration (228 objects missing entirely, 156 inaccurately boxed with 0<IoU<0.5) plus 85 original boxes judged false positives; base detectors used for error proposals saturate at 186 (YOLOX) and 260 (Cascade R-CNN) of 330 validated missing objects, so up to 44% of missing labels go undetected under default matching and up to 66% under relaxed matching (no minimum box size).

verdicts.evidence: Primary source: Tkachenko, Thyagarajan & Mueller, 'ObjectLab: Automated Diagnosis of Mislabeled Images in Object Detection Data' (arXiv 2309.00832), read via ar5iv HTML. Sub-claim checks: (1) COCO-bench size/classes — CONFIRMED: "This subset of 2171 images from the famous COCO 2017 dataset only considers 5 of the classes" (person, chair, cup, car, traffic light). (2) 251 mislabeled (11.6%) — CONFIRMED: "251 images in COCO-bench are considered mislabeled"; 251/2171 = 11.56%, so 11.6% is a correct rounding (the paper states the count, not the percentage). (3) Precision@100 'between roughly 0.49 and 0.71 on its COCO-bench' — REFUTED as stated / partially correct: the 0.49 figure is ObjectLab's Precision@100 on COCO-bench with Detectron2 X-101 (Table 3: AP 0.365 / P@100 0.49 / P@NumErrors 0.34); with Faster-RCNN it is 0.43 (AP 0.273 / P@100 0.43 / P@NumErrors 0.30). The 0.71 figure is NOT a COCO-bench result: Table 1 ("Precision@100 achieved by various label quality scores for detecting mislabeled images in the COCO-full dataset", the full 118k-image COCO 2017 train set with 80 classes) reports ObjectLab 0.71 (Detectron-X101) and 0.57 (Faster-RCNN) vs the mAP baseline 0.22 / 0.17. So the correct COCO-bench range is 0.43–0.49, and the 0.57–0.71 range belongs to COCO-full. Precision@100 is defined as the fraction of the 100 lowest-scoring images that are truly mislabeled. Baselines on COCO-bench P@100: mAP 0.20 (X-101) / 0.26 (FRCNN), Tile-estimates 0.26 / 0.32, CLOD 0.18 / 0.16. (4) ~5% overlooked / ~3% badly located / ~0.7% incorrect class — CONFIRMED with a caveat on provenance: "Through visual examination of many top/mid/bottom-ranking ObjectLab results, we estimate that in COCO 2017 around: 5% of images have an Overlooked error, 3% have a Badly Located error, and 0.7% have a Swapped error." This is an informal visual-inspection estimate (sample size and extrapolation method not stated), not a measured statistic, and the paper's term is 'Swapped' rather than 'incorrect class'. The cleanlab blog post and arXiv abstract page do not contain these numbers; only the full paper does.
verdicts.corrected_claim: ObjectLab (Tkachenko, Thyagarajan & Mueller, arXiv 2309.00832) evaluates on COCO-bench, a 2,171-image subset of COCO 2017 covering 5 classes (person, chair, cup, car, traffic light) in which 251 images (11.6%) were adjudicated as mislabeled; on COCO-bench ObjectLab's Precision@100 (fraction of the 100 lowest-scoring images that are truly mislabeled) is 0.49 with Detectron2 X-101 and 0.43 with Faster-RCNN (vs mAP baseline 0.20/0.26), while on the full 118k-image COCO 2017 train set ('COCO-full') it reaches 0.71 and 0.57 (vs mAP 0.22/0.17); the authors also state, based on informal visual examination of ObjectLab rankings, that roughly 5% of COCO 2017 images have an overlooked-object error, 3% a badly located box, and 0.7% a swapped class label.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Human bounding-box agreement ceilings from primary sources: on PASCAL VOC 2007, ground-truth boxes agree with boxes fitted to the ground-truth segmentation masks at 88% mean IoU, with 93% of boxes above IoU 0.7, and perturbing each box coordinate by 4 px likewise yields 88% mIoU (Papadopoulos et al., ICCV 2017, Sec. 5.1) — a figure the Open Images V4 paper later cites as 'human expert agreement is 0.88' (no separate two-expert box study exists); LVIS measured a dataset-average mask IoU of 0.85 (and F1 0.87) between two independent annotation runs of the 5,000 COCO val2017 images, and 0.90–0.92 mean mask IoU against expert annotators (Gupta et al., 2019, Sec. 4.2); Open Images' semi-automatic (box-verification) boxes were accepted only if judged to have IoU > 0.7 with an imaginary perfect box, and in practice have mean IoU ~0.82 (not 0.77), with such boxes making up ~10% of V4 training boxes.
